transcript.text: There are some core things that are
really important to understand when you
are working on your recovery from a
condition where nervous system
regulation is at the core of what's
going on. And right now I'm going to
walk you through what one of those
things are. It's something that I find
that even many of the experts in this
space who are very wellinformed about
brain retraining actually don't talk
about this one critical piece. And
without addressing this, as you work on
your recovery, you are pretty much
setting yourself up for a scenario where
symptoms will keep coming back. Trust
me, I know this from experience. So, I
think most of us are starting to
understand by now that symptoms have a
purpose. They are a tool that our brain
and our nervous system use to alert us
to some sort of threat. This can be an
emotional threat or a physical threat.
As the incredible Dr. Howard Schubiner
explained in my interview with him, it
is the exact same neural pathways in the
brain that are enacted. Whether it's a
physical threat or an emotional threat,
it's all processed the same. And once
that threat is detected, it uses what it
has at its disposal to let you know that
you need to pay attention, which is to
give you symptoms. And those symptoms
will stay. You'll keep having them until
your brain and your nervous system
assess that the threat is no longer
there. I often use the example of a
building with a fire alarm going off.
That alarm, that's that building's
symptom to alert you. That alarm will
keep going off as long as its sensors
detect that there's still a fire in the
building. And then once the sensors
detect that there's no more fire,
there's no more smoke, then it will turn
the alarm off. So if you still have
symptoms, if there are still symptoms in
your body, your brain and your nervous
system are still assessing that there is
a threat. That is a fact. And until you
can signal to your brain and your
nervous system that there is no threat,
those symptoms will keep coming up. And
there are two main ways that we can
signal to our brain and our nervous
system that there is no threat and we do
not need these horrible symptoms. And
the first one we talk about a lot and
that is our reaction to symptoms. So
when symptoms come up, if we respond
with fear and panic and oh my goodness,
what's going on? Or if we're like
frustrated, why are they still here? All
these negative emotions that is telling
those sensors in our body, yeah, we
still got a problem. things are not
okay, keep the symptoms going. So yes,
it's very important to work to respond
to your symptoms in a different way, in
a way that you feel safe, that you
remember that your body is okay and that
you're not continually continuing to set
off those alarms or to reinforce to your
brain and your nervous system that those
alarms are still needed. But on this
one, here's the insight that changes
everything. You can be reacting to your
symptoms with neutrality and lightness
and acceptance all day long every day.
And if you're not doing this second
thing, your symptoms might get less.
They might even go away, but they're
going to continue to come back. And the
second piece of this is something of
everything I've read, of everyone I've
talked to, everyone I've interviewed,
the person who explains this the best is
the incredible Nicole Sax. She's an
absolute guru in this space and for good
reason. She's been doing this work for
decades and helped thousands of people
to get past their mindbody conditions.
And she talks about the second thing
that's setting off those alarm bells for
your brain and your nervous system is
your emotional reservoir. and she
explains this um like to help you to
understand what this is and why it's an
issue and why you need to address it.
Picture a beaker inside of your chest
like one of those big glass beers that
they use in laboratories and we have
this and this is where we store emotions
that we haven't processed, we haven't
dealt with, we've pushed down for
whatever reason. We can get some strong
emotions that we don't want to deal
with. We're like, "Ah, we'll just shove
them down." or our boss is mean to us,
like just put it down. Or maybe we're
living a life that doesn't really make
us happy or we're not being our
authentic selves in the world and we
keep showing up and putting on this mask
and um pretending that everything's okay
and it's not okay and we shove it down.
We shove it down. This can be things
from our past. This can be trauma from
our childhood um that we haven't that
we're scared to deal with that we don't
think about or we we don't even realize
that we need to process it cuz we think
that's in the past. How is that
affecting me now? So, we shove it down
and we shove it down and we're built
with this beaker. It's a tool of ours.
It's a good thing. We need this. It
helps us. Repressing mo emotions is
something that we do. It's an adaptive
response because we don't want to feel
every strong emotion in the moment that
we get it. Like picture that your boss
is having a bad day and goes off on you
in a meeting in like in front of all of
your colleagues and you are filled
instantly with explosive rage. Like do
you want to start swearing and throwing
things around the room and quit your job
and slam the door? Like probably not
even though it would feel good in that
moment. So, it helps us to be like, I'm
going to put this away for now, and I'm
going to deal with it when I'm in a
safer space to process this emotion. So,
it's a good thing that we do this.
Here's where the problem happens. If
that beaker starts to fill up, if it
reaches a maximum density, it's about to
overflow, there's too much. We haven't
been dealing with things for far too
long. That sends off alarm bells. our
brain and our nervous system register
that the same way that it would register
the threat of a person chasing us with a
gun. Remember, emotional threats,
physical threats processed by the brain
the exact same way. So, we need tools to
deal with this emotional reservoir that
we have. We need ways to take scoops out
of it so it stays at a manageable level
and our brain and our nervous system are
like, "Yeah, that's okay. It's there. We
know it's there. It's fine. It's not a
danger. We've got this under control.
And the good news is is we're never
trying to get it empty. No one's ever
going to be like, I've dealt with all my
trauma and processed all my emotions and
I'm in this perfectly pristine place of
serenity and peace. That is not what
we're aiming for. We are resilient. You
can handle stress. You can store some
emotions away for later. That is fine.
But you need to make sure that you're
dealing with them eventually. And there
are so many different ways that you can
do this. You can do this through
journaling, which is one of the ones
that Nicole Sax talks about a lot, and
really honest journaling where you're
not just recounting your days or your
frustrations, but you're shining a light
on the parts of your thoughts and your
feelings that you think you're not
allowed to have, that you think are
shameful or wrong or just so terrible
that you can't admit them out loud. And
you can just write them down and then
set that journal on fire. You never have
to read it again. No one ever has to see
it. But it's important to get it out.
And this can be through therapy. This
can be through meditation. This can be
through screaming into a pillow. It can
be having really honest conversations
with people in your life that you trust.
Just finding ways to take those scoops
out. And the incredible thing is is that
just giving your emotions space frees up
that um emotional reservoir, that beaker
that you're carrying around. Because
emotions just eventually want and need
to be felt. And something magical
happens when you allow yourself to feel
an emotion. An emotion felt is emotion
changed. You feel it get lighter. You
feel yourself start to release it. You
see yourself like learn things from it
and figure out how to do things better
in the future. Without using these tools
to address your emotional reservoir,
your symptoms are going to keep coming
back. They might disappear for a while,
but then they're going to pop up again.
And they might look different. They
might be in a new spot. They might be a
completely new symptom. But your brain
and your nervous system are going to
continue to do what they're meant to do.
What you want them to do is to alert you
to danger. And the tool they have for
that is symptoms. And once you've dealt
with these first things, so you've
figured out the tools to respond to you
to your symptoms without fear. And now
you've got all these tools to deal with
your emotional reservoir. From there,
the third step is just uh figuring out
learning how to slowly expand activity
and resume normal activity while feeling
safe doing it. Because we also become
fearful about everything in life. We
start to associate exercise, danger,
like going outside, I'm going to feel
worse, sitting up too long, um you know,
talking on the phone too long, whatever
it is. We become very fearful of life.
But it's okay because we can rewire that
as well and we can teach our brain and
our nervous system that these things are
safe. Also, if you'd like to learn more
about this, I invite you to come join me
in my course. I have a course called
brain retraining 101 for ME/CFS and
longcoid recovery. Now, virtually all
the information and resources that I
have, you can find for free online in
various formats. It is all there. But if
you want to save yourself some digging,
um you can come and join me in the
course and you just have all the
essential need to know information in
one place. And it's also a place where
you can connect with a supportive
community. We have weekly live group
coaching calls that I do that other
coaches do. And uh I look forward to
meeting you if you do join. And you'll
just also have these amazing people
around you who get it and are supporting
you and are cheering you on as you work
your way past this. Thank you for
watching and if you'd like to join the
course, there's a link in the video
description to learn more and I hope to
see you there.
